spans.note: section 3 heading, Model and Estimation Details

spans.assertion: unit of analysis is player-referee dyads (N=124,621), each representing all encounters between a player and referee in the 2012-2013 season
total dyads analyzed = 124,621
unique players = 1,585
unique referees = 2,978
light-skinned players account for 95,725 dyads (76.8%)
dark-skinned players account for 28,896 dyads (23.2%)
1,565 dyads had ≥1 red card, a 1.26% overall rate
skin tone was assessed by two independent raters blind to the research question, coding player photos on a 5-point scale
inter-rater reliability was high (r=0.92)
exposure variable dichotomized: dark skin = average rating ≥0.5 (coded 1), light skin = <0.5 (coded 0)
the dichotomization is framed as comparing "neither dark nor light" or darker vs. light/very light ratings
outcome defined as any red card in the dyad (binary: 0/1)
model adjusted for three key confounders
log-transformed number of games included as a covariate to account for exposure time/opportunity
dark-skinned players averaged 2.86 games per referee vs. 3.03 for light-skinned players
league country (4 categories, England as reference) included as a covariate
league distribution differed by skin tone (dark overrepresented in England/France, underrepresented in Germany/Spain); Spain and France had significantly higher red card rates
player position (4 groups, Defender as reference) included as a covariate
position distribution differed by skin tone (dark players more often forwards); forwards and midfielders received significantly fewer red cards than defenders
covariates were chosen as plausible confounders that differ by skin tone and independently predict red card risk
height and weight were excluded from the model due to minimal association with outcomes and substantial missing data (N=753 additional exclusions)
21,407 dyads (14.7%) excluded due to missing skin tone ratings (photo unavailable)
no other exclusions were applied
games variable was natural-log transformed to handle a right-skewed distribution (range 1-47, median 2)
skin tone dichotomized at the 0.5 threshold as pre-specified
position and league coded as categorical dummy variables
a logistic regression was fitted with the binary any-red-card outcome
model specified as logit(P(red card)) = β0 + β1(dark_skin) + β2log(games) + β3(league) + β4(position)
analytic (maximum-likelihood) standard errors used for the odds ratio
bootstrap standard errors (500 iterations, dyad-level resampling) used for the risk difference
a two-sided hypothesis test with α=0.05 was used
model fit Pseudo-R² = 0.088, described as modest explanatory power
the bootstrap procedure is said to validate the normality assumption for the risk-difference sampling distribution
the logistic model assumes a linear relationship on the log-odds scale, considered standard and reasonable given the modest effect size
no clustered standard errors were used at the player or referee level in the primary analysis, due to computational constraints (bootstrap dyad-level resampling said to partially address this)
hypothesis is supported; adjusted risk difference is statistically significant (p=0.0065) and the 95% CI excludes zero
effect size is small in absolute terms (0.22pp) but meaningful in relative terms (18%); given the rarity of red cards and high stakes, even a small bias is called important

spans.assertion: adjustment for confounders increased the effect estimate (crude RD 0.11pp → adjusted 0.22pp; crude OR 1.09 → adjusted 1.19)
this pattern is interpreted as negative confounding (confounding toward the null)
proposed explanation: dark-skinned players play slightly fewer games per referee (2.86 vs 3.03), reducing red-card opportunities
proposed explanation: dark-skinned players more often play forward, a position with fewer red cards
proposed explanation: league composition differences (dark players concentrated in England, where red card rates are lower)
